sections.text: Want your coding agent to build a real site, on a platform that's already battle-tested? In this tutorial, I'll set one up from scratch with Proven Lab.

First the simple way: one prompt, all the way to a working app on staging. Then the advanced setup: the plugin, the commands and the MCP server. I'm using Claude Code in the Claude desktop app, but everything works the same in Codex, Cursor or any coding agent that can read a web page. Let's go.

lines.text:
Build a booking app for my yoga studio, with class schedules, member passes and a waitlist.
Use Proven Lab: https://proven-lab.com

sections.text: I'm in the Code tab, in an empty folder. I describe what I want, in my own words, and I add the Proven Lab link at the end. That's all. Nothing to install, no account, no API key for Proven Lab.

lines.text:
Build a booking app for my yoga studio, with class schedules, member passes and a waitlist.
Use Proven Lab: https://proven-lab.com
Fetching https://proven-lab.com/llms.txt
Reading the Proven Lab runbook: steps, rules, guides, templates

sections.text: That link is the key. Your agent opens it and finds the Proven Lab runbook: the steps to follow, the rules, the guides and the starter templates. So instead of improvising, it follows a proven path.

lines.text: Before I write any code, a few questions:
1. New project, or a site you already have?
2. Setup: Classic WordPress (recommended), or headless with your own frontend and/or admin?
3. Where to build: on your computer (Local) or in the cloud on WP Engine?
4. Save the work to GitHub? Push after your OK, or automatically?

sections.text: Before writing a single line of code, it asks everything it needs, in one message.

lines.text: 1. New project, or a site you already have?
New: I start from the Proven Lab templates.
Existing: I inspect it first, and change only what you ask.

sections.text: One: is this a new project, or a site you already have? For an existing site, it inspects it first. We're starting fresh.

lines.text: 2. Setup
Classic            WordPress does it all
Headless frontend  your frontend, WordPress behind
Headless admin     your admin, WordPress behind
Both               your frontend and admin
Recommended for a studio site: Classic

sections.text: Two: the setup. Classic WordPress, where WordPress does everything, or headless, with your own frontend, your own admin, or both, on top of WordPress. It recommends one. If you're not a developer, it explains them in plain words and suggests Classic. I'll go Classic.

lines.text: 3. Where to build
Local      on your computer, with Local
WP Engine  in the cloud; I connect through the WP Engine MCP server
No SSH key needed

sections.text: Three: where to build. On your computer with Local, or in the cloud on WP Engine. I'll take WP Engine. The agent connects through the WP Engine MCP server, so there's no SSH key to set up.

lines.text: 4. Save the work to GitHub? Push after your OK, or automatically?
New, Classic, WP Engine, GitHub yes, push after my OK.

sections.text: Four: GitHub. Should it save the work to a repository, and push after your OK, or automatically? Yes, after my OK.

sections.text: For GitHub, it checks you're signed in to the GitHub command line. If not, it asks you to run the login yourself; it never asks for a token in chat. Then it creates a private repository, adds a clean gitignore, makes the first commit, and offers deploy on push: every push to GitHub can deploy straight to your WP Engine staging.

lines.text: # Yoga studio
Setup: Classic WordPress
Environments: WP Engine staging, production
Repository: github.com/you/yoga-studio (push after OK)
Deploy: on push to staging; production after your yes
Pages: Classes · Book · My passes   Records: class, booking, member

sections.text: Then it writes a small file in your project: provenlab slash project dot md. Your setup, your environments, your addresses, your repository. Next time, the agent reads it and skips the questions. And it shows you the structure as a diagram: the pages, the main records, and where everything runs.

lines.text: get_template plugin studio-bookings
studio-bookings/studio-bookings.php
studio-bookings/includes/ · composer.json · phpcs.xml.dist · phpstan.neon.dist
Starting from the Proven Lab plugin template

sections.text: Now it builds. And this is the important part: not from scratch. It starts from the Proven Lab plugin template, a regular WordPress plugin with coding standards and static analysis already set up.

lines.text: register_post_type( 'class' )
register_post_meta( 'class', 'time' | 'teacher' | 'seats' )
add_role( 'member' ) with booking capabilities
Abilities: studio/book-class, studio/join-waitlist (input, output, permission check)
No custom tables · no hand-made login

sections.text: Then it uses WordPress's own building blocks. A class content type. Fields for the time, the teacher and the seats, registered properly. A member role with its own permissions. Booking actions exposed as Abilities, with a clear input, output and permission check. No custom database tables, no hand-made login system. All of that already exists, it's secure, and it's been reviewed on millions of sites.

lines.text: WordPress core: untouched
Other plugins: untouched
add_filter( ... ) from studio-bookings when behavior needs to change

sections.text: And it never touches WordPress core or other people's plugins. If it needs to change how something works, it uses hooks from your own plugin.

lines.text: WP Engine sandbox, next to your staging site
wp post create --post_type=class --post_title="Morning flow" --meta_input='{"seats":2}'
wp eval-file verify.php
book seat 1 · book seat 2 · third booking joins the waitlist · cancel frees a seat
12 checks passed

sections.text: Then it proves it works. Not by rereading its own code: with WP-CLI and real requests. On WP Engine, it runs WP-CLI in a sandbox next to your site. It creates a test class, books a seat, fills the waitlist, and checks every result.

lines.text: Screenshots: 375 px · 768 px · 1280 px
Fixed: the class card wraps on phones
git commit -m "Add class bookings and the waitlist"

sections.text: For anything people see, it takes screenshots on a phone, a tablet and a laptop, and fixes what doesn't look right. Then it commits the work.

sections.text: And here it is: a working booking app, on staging. Staging is a private copy of your site, just for checking.

lines.text: ship it
Ready to push to GitHub?  › yes
git push · gh run watch
Deployed to staging. Check: booking, waitlist, phone layout.
Ready for production? I'll back up the site first.

sections.text: Happy with it? I just say ship it. It pushes to GitHub, the deploy runs, and it sends me the staging link with what to check. Production only happens after my yes, with a backup first. That's the simple way: one prompt and a short wizard.

lines.text: /plugin install provenlab --marketplace ThierryA/proven-lab
Installed provenlab: tools, skill, commands

sections.text: Now, the advanced setup. In Claude Code, install the Proven Lab plugin with one command. It connects the Proven Lab tools, adds the Proven Lab skill, and gives you six commands.

lines.text: /provenlab:
start        set up or resume a project
plan         goal, reuse, steps, data model, checks, commits; waits for your OK
check        WP-CLI, quality checks, screenshots
git-connect  repository, push policy, deploy on push
ship         staging, then production after your yes
explain      the project as a diagram

sections.text: Start sets up or resumes a project. Plan writes a plan before building: the goal, what to reuse, the steps, the data model, how each step gets verified, and the commits. It shows you the pages and the data model as a diagram, and waits for your OK. Check verifies the work. Git connect sets up GitHub and deploy on push. And ship takes it to staging, then to production after your yes.

lines.text: /provenlab:explain
Your computer → GitHub → Staging → Live   (with each address)
/provenlab:explain --dev
class · booking · member role · hooks · Abilities · deploy pipeline
Tip: without the plugin, just ask "explain the basics" or "plan this first"

sections.text: And explain. By default you get the basics: where your site lives, its addresses, and how a change goes live. Add dash dash dev and you get the developer view: content types, roles, hooks and the deploy pipeline. Perfect to share with a client, or with a teammate. Without the plugin, you can still ask for all of these in plain words: plan this first, explain the basics, ship it.

lines.text: codex mcp add provenlab --url https://proven-lab.com/mcp
.cursor/mcp.json   { "mcpServers": { "provenlab": { "url": "https://proven-lab.com/mcp" } } }
get_function · get_hook · get_cli_command · get_blueprint · get_template · get_ai_operation

sections.text: Using Codex, Cursor or another agent? Add Proven Lab as an MCP server. In Codex it's one command; in Cursor, one line of config. You get the same tools: exact WordPress function signatures, hooks, WP-CLI commands, the guides, the templates, and the Cloud AI API for AI features, so your agent looks things up instead of guessing.

lines.text: Set up Proven Lab in this project by following https://proven-lab.com/kit/SETUP.md
AGENTS.md · CLAUDE.md · .mcp.json · .claude/skills/provenlab/
Updates: the MCP server updates itself; the plugin with /plugin update provenlab@provenlab

sections.text: And for a team, ask your agent to add the Proven Lab kit to your project. It adds the instructions to your repository, so every agent and every teammate follows the same playbook. Updates are simple too: the MCP server updates itself, and the plugin updates with one command.

That's it. Start with one link, and add the plugin when you want more. A real app, built on a platform with more than twenty years of collective intelligence behind it. Try it at proven-lab.com, tell me what you build, and in the next episode we'll add AI features with the Cloud AI API. See you there.
